title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (study id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The experiment used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter with shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The confirmatory sample comprised 200 intent→configuration tasks (4 topology clusters × 50 tasks each). Execution used 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because baseline validator‑detected failures were 0% on this bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, complete execution accounting, representative diagnostics, contamination check evidence (10% Mininet holdout = 20 tasks; zero validator–emulator disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models can increase NetOps productivity but creates risk: incorrect or unsafe configurations can cause outages, policy violations, or degraded service. A common architectural mitigation is generate–validate–repair (GVR): the LLM produces a candidate configuration, a deterministic validator checks it, and if violations are reported the LLM is prompted to repair the same candidate. The practical value of automated repair therefore depends on three factors: (i) the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures produced by the chosen generator and prompting policy; (ii) the validator’s coverage and fidelity to end‑to‑end device behavior; and (iii) the repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered the narrow confirmatory question: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Our contributions are (1) a sealed preregistered paired experiment that enforces shared‑initial generation to isolate the effect of validator+repair on an identical generated candidate; (2) a complete archival execution with deterministic reconciliation and full accounting (complete pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0); and (3) an artifact‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome together with operational recommendations and reproducibility notes.
sections.related_work: Prior work documents that LLMs exhibit factual errors and prompt sensitivity and that grounding, retrieval augmentation, and verifier‑assisted repair can reduce factual mistakes. Prototype intent→configuration systems demonstrate feasibility for translating natural language intent into device configurations or orchestration steps, but instrumented production‑scale failure‑rate studies are scarce. Architectural proposals integrate deterministic network validators (e.g., Batfish or domain‑specific checkers) into generation workflows; empirical red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies show that tool‑description injection and tool‑chaining can change safety outcomes materially. Surveys and evaluations therefore recommend external, preregistered measurement designs that isolate the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair for a fixed model and prompt policy. Our study positions itself within this stream by measuring a pre‑specified paired estimand under controlled shared‑initial generation semantics and by archiving the full execution and analysis artifacts for independent scrutiny.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study preregistration (id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02; preregistration_sha256: a9e5d64cbe3a888170d614b971313b4f1550707d39db945843bca930d8caf5d6) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, up to one repair call per task (repair budget = 1), and a single primary confirmatory test: exact McNemar two‑sided (α = 0.05) on paired binary outcomes (validator pass/fail). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; 95% CIs were computed with a bootstrap percentile method (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and target 50% relative reduction, yielding approximate 0.8 power at n = 200 under those assumptions; these assumptions were frozen pre‑execution.

Task bank and validators. The confirmatory sample used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial/expected final states, workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, atomic MTU changes), and an explicit required_sequence to make intent checks deterministic. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces the task‑encoded constraints and emits structured diagnostics (valid boolean, violation_codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; its execution and summary are archived.

Model and generation semantics. The experiment used the hosted model declared in the preregistration (gpt‑5‑mini) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Crucially, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each pair the system produced a single initial candidate which was deterministically reused for both the baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This isolates the marginal effect of validator+repair by removing per‑condition sampling variance and ensuring that any repair activity must operate on the same initial string.

Repair policy, budgets and contamination handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed one automated repair prompt to the same LLM if the primary validator reported violations; up to 200 repair calls were therefore allowed but only if initial candidates failed validation. The contamination_plan deterministically excluded pairs where the primary validator disagreed with the Mininet emulator; preregistered sensitivity analyses specified alternative treatments of flagged tasks. Missingness and stopping rules were fixed before execution; any infrastructure failures would be logged and treated per the predefined missingness_plan.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed as planned: planned_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation for each of 200 pairs reused across conditions), completed_episode_count = 400, complete_pair_count = 200, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), repair_calls_used = 0. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts report hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, and all deterministic consistency checks passed (pair_accounting_consistent = true).

Descriptive outcomes and primary test. The deterministic validator accepted every initial candidate: baseline_success_count = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0) and guarded_success_count = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. With no discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0] as computed in the preregistered analysis executor.

Repair activity, contamination checks, and examples. Because no initial candidate failed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the GVR pipeline issued zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% of tasks = 20 tasks) executed and the contamination summary reports zero validator–emulator disagreement flags for that holdout. Representative examples (artifact pairs pair‑000001 through pair‑000006) show shared initial generator outputs that matched the task required_sequence; their validator_trace.validation_after.valid flags are true and violation_count = 0 despite difficulty annotations that label several tasks as medium→very_hard (e.g., make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). Secondary/exploratory estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate) are empty because no repair events occurred; the analysis bundle records these secondary_results as empty.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the degenerate confirmatory outcome. The observed degenerate result is scientifically informative: when a fixed model plus prompt policy and the enforced shared_initial semantics produce validator‑passing candidates for every item in a workload, a validator‑coupled repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This outcome does not mean that GVR is universally useless—rather, GVR’s marginal operational benefit depends on nontrivial baseline validator failure prevalence and on validator coverage.

Artifact‑grounded reasons for zero baseline failures. The archived evidence supports multiple non‑exclusive explanations: (1) the prompt template and shared_initial deterministic sampling policy produced candidates that exactly matched the explicit task bank constraints; (2) the curated task bank encodes explicit required_sequences that are straightforward for a constrained prompt policy to satisfy; (3) the primary validator enforces the task‑encoded constraints but may omit device‑level or vendor idiosyncrasies that only an emulator or real device could reveal; (4) the shared_initial design intentionally removed per‑condition re‑sampling as a pathway for generating alternative, possibly repairable candidates.

Operational implications. Practitioners should measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workloads before investing in automated repair infrastructure. If baseline failures are rare, resources may be better spent on improving validator fidelity (richer device semantics and vendor models), adversarial testing, multi‑sample or multi‑model generation policies, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals. Conversely, when baseline failures are non‑negligible, GVR can reduce validator‑detected issues; realized gains will depend on repair budget, prompt engineering for repair, validator completeness, and whether validators capture end‑to‑end device behavior.

Reproducibility, contamination check gap, and archival evidence. All key execution artifacts (model‑call logs, validator traces, paired contingency tables, bootstrap parameters) are archived in the execution bundle and the analysis artifacts (for example, analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) directly record the reported counts and rates. The Mininet contamination summary indicates the holdout was executed (20 tasks) and reports zero disagreements; however, an explicit labeled artifact recording the randomized selection seed for the Mininet holdout is absent from the labeled archive, which prevents bit‑exact reconstruction of the exact randomized draw despite the contamination summary evidence of zero disagreements. We report this reproducibility gap transparently and include the contamination summary evidence that no disagreements were observed.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is supported by preregistration, adapter enforcement of shared_initial semantics, and deterministic stopping rules; however, the shared_initial choice trades generality for controlled isolation and removed per‑condition sampling variance. Construct validity: the primary validator checks task‑encoded constraints but can miss device idiosyncrasies or emergent behaviors only visible under end‑to‑end execution. External validity: results reflect a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), one deterministic sampling policy, and a curated task bank; extrapolation to other models, higher temperature sampling, multi‑sample strategies, adversarial distributions, or real device fleets is not supported by these artifacts. Conclusion validity: the McNemar test is uninformative when discordant pairs are zero, yet the observed degenerate outcome is itself an operationally meaningful datum that should guide future workload selection and power planning.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was not testable because the baseline failure rate was 0% on this bank. This outcome emphasizes that the marginal value of automated repair is workload dependent: when baseline validator failures are rare, repair yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future work should evaluate GVR on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, extend validator fidelity with richer emulator or real‑device checks, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model generation policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived for independent inspection in the execution bundle referenced by the preregistration metadata.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory Disclosure. This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 (preregistration SHA‑256: a9e5d64cbe3a888170d614b971313b4f1550707d39db945843bca930d8caf5d6). LLMs and frameworks used: hosted model = gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family; code and orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; the primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba), as required by the track. Topic constraints imposed by the human Research Director limited the run to Generative AI/LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Preregistration/freeze procedure: the experimental plan (paired design, n = 200, shared_initial generation semantics, estimand, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were permitted but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Secondary disagreement detector and holdout: a Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the analysis contamination summary reports zero validator–emulator disagreements. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary recording zero disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
